triage.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
triage.reason: Newborn with severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest; diagnosed by exam and chest x-ray, a classic neonatal emergency.

age.peak: newborn period (first hours to days of life)

demographics: Occurs in about 1 in 2,500 to 1 in 5,000 live births
Most cases are diagnosed prenatally on ultrasound or immediately after birth
Rare late-presenting cases occur in older infants and young children

risk_factors.text: Prenatal ultrasound findings of herniated abdominal contents in the chest, mediastinal shift, or polyhydramnios
Family history of congenital diaphragmatic hernia or other congenital diaphragmatic defects
Associated congenital anomalies (cardiac, renal, skeletal, or chromosomal)
Maternal exposure to teratogens such as phenytoin, thalidomide, or retinoids during pregnancy

comorbidities: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
family_history: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia in a sibling or parent
exposures: Maternal teratogen exposure during pregnancy (phenytoin, thalidomide, retinoids)

chief_complaints.text: My baby is breathing very fast and hard
My baby's lips and fingers look blue
My baby's belly looks flat and sunken

hpi.onset: At birth or within the first few hours of life; often noted immediately in the delivery room
hpi.progression: Rapidly worsening respiratory distress over minutes to hours; may initially respond to oxygen but then deteriorate as pulmonary hypertension develops
hpi.quality: Labored, grunting, retracting breathing with nasal flaring
hpi.severity: Severe to critical; often requires immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation

atypical.how_it_differs: Older infants and children with a late-presenting defect may have mild chronic respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms such as recurrent vomiting, abdominal pain, or failure to thrive rather than severe neonatal distress.
Premature infants may have milder initial symptoms that are attributed to prematurity, delaying diagnosis until a chest x-ray is obtained.

general.mild: Alert newborn with mild tachypnea and no distress at rest; feeding well
general.moderate: Tachypneic and grunting, mild retractions, but pink on room air or low-flow oxygen
general.severe: Labored breathing with grunting, retractions and nasal flaring; cyanotic, requires positive-pressure support
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or mottled, apneic or gasping, unresponsive to stimulation; requires immediate intubation

findings.finding: Flat, sunken abdomen with a palpable costal margin
Bowel sounds heard over the left hemithorax
Decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Observe and count the respiratory rate for one full minute
findings.finding: Respiratory rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Observe and listen to the newborn's breathing
findings.finding: Grunting expiratory sound

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest wall during breathing
findings.finding: Inward pulling of the intercostal spaces with each breath
Flaring of the alae nasi with each breath

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue and nail beds
findings.finding: Bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and count the rate for one full minute
findings.finding: Heart rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart sounds at the apex and base
findings.finding: Heart sounds are soft and difficult to hear

findings.maneuver: Palpate the precordium for the point of maximal impulse
findings.finding: Apical impulse displaced to the right of the sternum

findings.finding: Trachea deviated away from the side of the hernia

findings.maneuver: Press the nail bed or sternum and release, timing the return of color

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant's level of alertness and response to stimulation
findings.finding: Reduced alertness and responsiveness
No heart murmur

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for the liver edge
findings.finding: Liver not palpable below the costal margin
Temperature within the normal range

labs.caveat: Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation and CO2 retention; a low pH with a normal or high PaCO2 points to respiratory failure rather than a primary metabolic problem.
Rising PaCO2 despite oxygen is a sign of worsening hypoventilation and impending respiratory failure.
Hypoxemia is often refractory to supplemental oxygen because of right-to-left shunting through the hypoplastic lung and persistent pulmonary hypertension.
A negative base excess reflects a metabolic component from poor perfusion and lactic acid production.
Elevated lactate suggests inadequate tissue perfusion from severe hypoxemia or low cardiac output.
A mild leukocytosis is common in the stressed newborn and does not by itself indicate infection.
Thrombocytopenia can occur with severe illness or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
A rising creatinine suggests poor renal perfusion or acute kidney injury from critical illness.
Not part of the newborn workup; included only for the rare adolescent or adult with a late-presenting defect in whom pregnancy must be excluded before imaging.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Right axis deviation
Right ventricular hypertrophy pattern (tall R waves in V1, deep S waves in V6)
Peaked P waves in lead II suggesting right atrial enlargement
Nonspecific ST-T wave changes from hypoxemia

imaging.preferred_when: First-line study in any newborn with respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen

findings.text: Bowel loops visible within the left hemithorax
Decreased or absent aerated lung on the affected side
Scaphoid abdomen with paucity of bowel gas below the diaphragm
Nasogastric tube coiled in the lower left chest

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or to avoid radiation in a stable infant

findings.text: Abdominal viscera (bowel, stomach, liver or spleen) seen above the diaphragm
Defect in the diaphragm with loss of the normal continuity

imaging.preferred_when: All infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia to assess pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac anomalies

findings.text: Right-to-left or bidirectional shunting across the patent ductus arteriosus
Right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale
Elevated right ventricular systolic pressure / pulmonary hypertension

imaging.study: CT chest and abdomen with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Rarely needed; may be used in late-presenting or atypical cases in older children

findings.text: Diaphragmatic defect with herniated abdominal contents
Lung hypoplasia on the affected side

imaging.preferred_when: Selected complex cases when detailed anatomy is needed without ionizing radiation

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis by showing bowel loops in the chest, mediastinal shift and a scaphoid abdomen
Assesses oxygenation, ventilation and acid-base status in a critically ill newborn
Baseline blood count and to look for anemia or infection
Baseline electrolytes, glucose and renal function before surgery
Assesses pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac anomalies

supporting.why: Confirms herniated viscera when the x-ray is equivocal or to avoid radiation
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain or the infant is stable

supporting.why: Marker of tissue perfusion in critical illness
supporting.only_if: there are signs of shock or poor perfusion

supporting.why: Monitors renal function in a critically ill infant
supporting.only_if: there is concern for acute kidney injury or poor urine output

not_indicated.test: CT chest and abdomen with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Rarely needed; the diagnosis is usually made by x-ray and ultrasound, and CT adds radiation
not_indicated.only_if: the diagnosis remains unclear in an older child with a late-presenting defect
complex anatomy requires detailed imaging without radiation

not_indicated.why: Not part of the newborn workup
not_indicated.only_if: the patient is an adolescent or adult who could be pregnant and imaging is planned

decision_points: Avoid bag-mask ventilation and place a nasogastric tube early to decompress the stomach and reduce bowel distension in the chest
Intubate and provide gentle ventilation; avoid high airway pressures that worsen the hypoplastic lung
Obtain an echocardiogram before surgery to assess pulmonary hypertension and cardiac anatomy
Correct acidosis, hypoxemia and hypotension before taking the infant to the operating room

differential.name: Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (congenital pulmonary airway malformation)
differential.why_considered: Prenatal cystic lung lesion with mediastinal shift and respiratory distress at birth
differential.trigger: Cystic lung mass on prenatal ultrasound or chest x-ray with mediastinal shift but a normal abdomen

history: Prenatal ultrasound showing a cystic lung mass rather than herniated bowel
exam: Normal abdominal contour and bowel sounds only in the abdomen
Decreased breath sounds on the affected side without bowel sounds in the chest
imaging: Chest x-ray shows multiple air-filled cysts or a solid lung mass confined to the thorax
Normal diaphragm and normal bowel gas pattern below the diaphragm
CT or MRI shows a lung lesion with intact diaphragm

differential.name: Congenital lobar emphysema
differential.why_considered: Hyperinflated lobe causing respiratory distress and mediastinal shift in a newborn
differential.trigger: Hyperlucent overexpanded lobe on chest x-ray with mediastinal shift but normal abdominal findings

history: Progressive tachypnea and grunting in the first days to weeks of life
No prenatal finding of abdominal contents in the chest
exam: Decreased breath sounds on the affected side without bowel sounds in the chest
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a hyperlucent, hyperexpanded lobe with compression of adjacent lung and mediastinal shift
Diaphragm is intact and bowel gas remains below it
CT confirms overdistended lobe with normal diaphragm

differential.name: Congenital diaphragmatic eventration
differential.why_considered: Elevated hemidiaphragm can mimic a diaphragmatic defect with respiratory symptoms

exam: Decreased breath sounds at the base on the affected side
Abdomen is usually normal, not scaphoid
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a smooth, elevated hemidiaphragm without bowel loops in the chest
Fluoroscopy or ultrasound shows paradoxical diaphragmatic movement without a defect
No herniated viscera above the diaphragm

differential.name: Congenital heart disease with cyanosis
differential.why_considered: Cyanosis and respiratory distress in a newborn
differential.trigger: Cyanosis with a murmur, abnormal pulses, or a normal chest x-ray without bowel in the chest

history: Cyanosis from birth or with feeding
May have a known prenatal cardiac anomaly
exam: Murmur, single second heart sound, or abnormal pulses
Bowel sounds only in the abdomen
labs: Hyperoxia test may show limited rise in PaO2
Blood gases show hypoxemia without CO2 retention typical of a cardiac shunt
imaging: Chest x-ray shows abnormal cardiac silhouette or pulmonary vascularity without bowel in the chest

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in a premature newborn with grunting and retractions

history: No prenatal finding of bowel in the chest
exam: Bowel sounds only in the abdomen
imaging: Chest x-ray shows diffuse ground-glass opacities and air bronchograms with low lung volumes
No bowel loops in the chest and normal diaphragm position

differential.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Tachypnea and mild respiratory distress shortly after birth

history: Often after cesarean delivery without labor
exam: Mild tachypnea without severe retractions or cyanosis
imaging: Chest x-ray shows perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures with normal diaphragm

differential.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in a newborn with a history of meconium-stained fluid

history: Often post-term or with fetal distress
exam: Meconium staining of skin, nails, and umbilical cord
imaging: Chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation
No bowel loops in the chest

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress, lethargy, and poor perfusion in a newborn
differential.trigger: Fever or hypothermia, lethargy, and risk factors for infection with respiratory distress

history: Maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, or group B streptococcus colonization
exam: Normal abdominal contour and bowel sounds only in the abdomen
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated CRP, positive blood culture
imaging: Chest x-ray may show pneumonia but no bowel in the chest

severity.mild: Mild respiratory distress with tachypnea and mild retractions, responding to low-flow oxygen; stable vital signs and no significant acidosis
severity.moderate: Moderate distress with grunting, retractions, and cyanosis requiring nasal CPAP or mechanical ventilation; mild respiratory acidosis
severity.severe: Severe distress with marked retractions, cyanosis, and respiratory acidosis requiring intubation and high-frequency ventilation; evidence of pulmonary hypertension
severity.critical: Cardiorespiratory failure with refractory hypoxemia, severe pulmonary hypertension, shock, and need for ECMO; high risk of death

red_flags.finding: Scaphoid abdomen with bowel sounds in the chest
red_flags.meaning: Strongly suggests congenital diaphragmatic hernia; avoid bag-mask ventilation and place a nasogastric tube
Right-to-left shunting from pulmonary hypertension; may need inhaled nitric oxide or ECMO
Impending respiratory failure; requires escalation of ventilatory support
Shock from severe hypoxemia or cardiac dysfunction; needs volume and inotropic support
Possible bowel strangulation or tension from herniated viscera; surgical emergency

complications.name: Pulmonary hypoplasia
clues: Small lung volumes on chest x-ray

complications.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

special_populations.differences: Premature infants may have milder initial symptoms attributed to prematurity, delaying diagnosis; they also have higher risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and need for prolonged ventilation.

Late-presenting defects in older infants and children often present with mild chronic respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms such as recurrent vomiting, abdominal pain, or failure to thrive rather than severe neonatal distress.

key_questions.question: When did the breathing difficulty start, and has it gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset at birth or within the first hours of life, with rapid worsening over minutes to hours

key_questions.question: Was the baby born at term or early, and how was the delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Gestational age, mode of delivery, and any fetal distress; prematurity may mask or delay the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Did the prenatal ultrasound show anything unusual, such as fluid around the baby or organs in the chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Prenatal findings of herniated abdominal contents in the chest, mediastinal shift, or polyhydramnios

key_questions.question: Does the baby's belly look flat or sunken?
key_questions.looking_for: A scaphoid abdomen, which suggests abdominal contents have moved into the chest

key_questions.question: Has the baby been feeding, and is there any vomiting or spitting up?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding; vomiting is uncommon early and may suggest a late-presenting or obstructive picture

key_questions.question: Has the baby had a fever, or any signs of infection around the time of birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or temperature instability; absence makes sepsis less likely but does not exclude it

key_questions.question: Does the baby have any other known birth defects or genetic conditions?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated cardiac, renal, skeletal, or chromosomal anomalies

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of congenital diaphragmatic hernia or other birth defects?
key_questions.looking_for: A sibling or parent with a congenital diaphragmatic defect

key_questions.question: Did the mother take any medications or have any exposures during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Teratogens such as phenytoin, thalidomide, or retinoids

key_questions.question: Has the baby's skin or lips looked blue at any point?
key_questions.looking_for: Cyanosis, especially if it does not improve with oxygen

key_questions.question: Has the baby been unusually sleepy or difficult to wake?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy, which may indicate severe hypoxemia or sepsis

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any coughing, wheezing, or noisy breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of these; their presence may point toward other respiratory causes

reasoning_points: A newborn with severe respiratory distress beginning at or shortly after birth
A scaphoid abdomen with bowel sounds heard in the chest on the affected side
Decreased breath sounds and possible mediastinal shift on examination
Chest x-ray showing bowel loops in the hemithorax, mediastinal shift, and paucity of bowel gas below the diaphragm
Echocardiogram showing pulmonary hypertension and excluding associated cardiac anomalies
Prenatal ultrasound findings of herniated abdominal contents or polyhydramnios
Recognition that this is a neonatal emergency requiring early nasogastric decompression and avoidance of bag-mask ventilation

easy: Term newborn with immediate severe respiratory distress
Scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the left chest
Chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the hemithorax with mediastinal shift
Prenatal ultrasound already showed herniated viscera
medium: Premature infant whose distress is initially attributed to prematurity
Mild tachypnea with subtle scaphoid abdomen and equivocal chest x-ray
Cyanosis with a normal abdominal contour, requiring echocardiogram to exclude congenital heart disease
Prenatal finding of mediastinal shift without a clear cause
hard: Late-presenting defect in an older infant with recurrent vomiting or failure to thrive
Older child with chronic respiratory symptoms and no acute distress
Newborn with concurrent sepsis or congenital heart disease obscuring the picture
Chest x-ray initially read as pneumonia or a cystic lung lesion
